extracted.intended_audience: general readers of 19th-century war memoirs; writers and historians interested in firsthand war reportage
extracted.subtask_description: A first-person, descriptive memoir of military campaigns and battles in the American Civil War emphasizing personal impressions, anecdotes, and on-the-ground scenes rather than exhaustive official military detail.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prefer personal impressions over exhaustive military detail
rubrics_metrics.description: "It is not my intention to give the details of the battle--the movements of each regiment, battalion, or battery, as it performed its part in the work. The official record will be sought by those who desire the purely military history."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If producing a memoir or personal account, emphasize eyewitness sensations, events, and character sketches rather than attempting a complete, regiment-by-regiment operational history; direct readers seeking precise military movements to official records.

rubrics_metrics.name: Record and communicate rules of campaign life and practical habits
rubrics_metrics.description: The author summarizes practical habits learned in the field: "I rarely moved without my blankets and rubber 'poncho,' and with a haversack more or less well filled."
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Include concrete, mundane details (gear, sleeping arrangements, common practices) to lend authenticity to campaign narratives and to orient readers to the practical realities of field life.

rubrics_metrics.name: Capture subjective sensory distortions under fire (time, distance, sound)
rubrics_metrics.description: The narrator repeatedly notes perceptual distortions: "Distances seemed much greater than they really were... The hours did not crowd into minutes, but the minutes almost extended into hours..." and describes vivid sounds (whistling of musket-balls, screech of shells).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use vivid sensory detail and acknowledge altered perceptions (time dilation, misjudged distances, distinctive sounds of projectiles) to convey the lived experience of battle; such subjective details are valuable even when they conflict with objective measures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use small anecdotes and concrete episodes to illustrate larger themes
rubrics_metrics.description: The narrative relies on short illustrative stories (the poisoned well, the White Cloud captain apologizing, the bear eating the honey, the soldier whittling a bullet) to reveal character and circumstance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Select brief, memorable vignettes that reveal social attitudes, discipline, or consequences; these episodic details communicate broader social and moral points more effectively than abstract statements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Acknowledge limits of eyewitness estimation and avoid overclaiming precision
rubrics_metrics.description: The author confesses to misjudging distances and durations (e.g., estimate of firing range) and explicitly separates his narrative from the 'official record.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When writing from direct experience, indicate uncertainty about numeric estimates (ranges, times, casualty figures) and, when necessary, point readers to official documents or reports for precise measurements; being candid about fallibility enhances credibility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Portray social complexity and divided loyalties through specific social details
rubrics_metrics.description: Observations on civilian sympathy and class differences: "the strongest secession sympathy was entertained by the wealthier inhabitants, while the poor were generally loyal," and on civilian conduct in hotels and on railways.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use concrete social details (economic status, local customs, public behavior) to represent the nuanced and often contradictory loyalties and customs of a region, rather than reducing populations to monolithic stereotypes.
